definition: Diffident means shy and hesitant from a lack of confidence in yourself.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word diffident. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know diffident should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Our most diffident analyst buries her sharpest ideas on the last slide, half hoping nobody will ask about them.
Humble is the milder virtue beside diffident — a humble champion credits her rivals yet still steps up to accept the trophy, while a diffident one doubts she should be on the stage at all.
Self-effacing goes further than humble—the self-effacing organizer edits herself out of the story entirely, while the diffident one hovers at its edge, doubting she belongs.

Unassuming describes a modest manner, whatever the confidence underneath — an unassuming expert may be perfectly sure of her work and simply not showy about it. Diffident points at the cause instead: the diffident hold back because their trust in their own ability runs short. Manner can be unassuming; diffidence is doubt.

Self-doubting names the engine outright: trust in yourself runs short. Diffident describes what that doubt does in company — the hesitant voice, the buried idea, the deflected credit. A self-doubting person might hide it completely; a diffident one shows it every time they hang back.

Okonkwo could never square the two versions of Sam she saw each Tuesday.
On paper he was the club's best programmer; his routing code ran twice as fast as anyone's.
In the room he was diffident to the point of vanishing -- hands half-raised then lowered, fixes offered as questions, every good idea hedged twice before he finished saying it.
It was not modesty, she decided, and it was not politeness; he genuinely did not believe his own results, however often the benchmarks repeated them.
So she stopped praising him publicly and started making him run the tests himself, twice, until the numbers became harder to argue with than his doubts were.
